name: Charlemagne
role: King of the Franks (768-814) and Emperor (800-814)
summary: Charlemagne expanded Frankish rule by conquest, incorporated the Lombard kingdom and subdued Saxony. His capitularies enforced Christian observance, directed religious education, required personal fidelity to the ruler and regulated access to grain in times of scarcity.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The 806 succession ordinance assigns entire kingdoms to his sons and preserves a route for a son’s child to inherit that kingdom.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: The 802 capitulary sets out legal consequences for unlawful marriages and requires kinship checks before couples can marry.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: The Nijmegen capitulary distinguishes royal benefices from allodial estates and recognizes the owners’ right to sell the latter’s surplus subject to a price ceiling.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Charlemagne treated conquered Lombardy as a kingdom over which he held the royal title and whose territory he could transfer by succession ordinance.

ban-interest.rationale: Chapter 5 of the Admonitio generalis prohibits lending at interest for everyone. The 806 Nijmegen decree defines the permissible return on a loan as the amount lent.

bound-labor.rationale: Chapter 4 of the 802 capitulary requires the return of fugitive royal serfs and prohibits concealing them. His estate instructions likewise treat dependent farm households as owing labor on the royal domains.

church-by-bishops.rationale: The 802 capitulary subjects priests and monasteries to episcopal authority and gives metropolitans oversight of bishops’ supervision of monasteries.

civil-marriage.rationale: The 802 capitulary requires clergy and elders to investigate the couple’s kinship before marriage and then prescribes a blessing for the marriage.

clerical-rule.rationale: As a lay ruler he appointed bishops alongside lay nobles as his envoys and reserved final judgment in cases those envoys could not resolve.

conscription.rationale: Chapter 7 of the 802 capitulary forbids men who owe military service to ignore a royal summons and bars counts from excusing them as a favor.

death-penalty.rationale: The Saxon capitulary orders death for refusing baptism, pagan burial, human sacrifice and conspiring with pagans (sections 5-13), so he applied capital punishment to serious offences including treason.

destroy-worshipped-objects.rationale: The royal annals record that Charlemagne destroyed the Saxon sanctuary at Irminsul in 772. The Frankfurt capitulary also directs adherence to canon law on the destruction of sacred trees and groves.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: In the preface to the Admonitio generalis, Charlemagne identifies divine grace as the source of his kingship and rule over the Frankish kingdom.

dynastic-succession.rationale: The 806 succession ordinance allocates the kingdoms to Charlemagne’s sons. In 813 he crowned Louis as co-emperor and named him his imperial heir.

elective-rulers.rationale: Charlemagne apportioned his kingdoms among his sons in 806 and designated Louis as imperial heir in 813. The 806 ordinance preserves a narrower role for the people in selecting a deceased son’s successor from within the dynasty.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Section 19 sets the fine for an unbaptized infant at 120 solidi for a noble, 60 for a freeman and 30 for a litus, so the same offence was punished according to rank.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: The royal annals record Charlemagne sending or leading armies against Saxons who rebelled after submitting to Frankish rule.

harm-principle.rationale: His Saxon capitulary imposes capital punishment for remaining unbaptized and for deliberately breaking the Lenten fast in contempt of Christianity.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The imperial capitulary makes military summonses his prerogative, and the annals record his personal command on campaign.

humans-entitled-to-use-animals.rationale: The royal estate ordinance directs stewards to maintain livestock and keep animals for provisioning the royal household.

indigenous-internal-justice.rationale: Chapter 4 of the 797 Saxon capitulary recognizes local settlement of Saxon cases by their neighbors under customary procedures, subject to review by the royal envoys or palace.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: After forcibly moving Saxon communities in 804, Charlemagne transferred their trans-Elbe districts to the Obodrites by imperial decision.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The Admonitio generalis expressly makes biblical commands the basis for royal rules on lending at interest, oaths and divination.

money-backed-by-precious-metals.rationale: Charlemagne’s 794 Frankfurt decree orders universal acceptance of his full-weight denarii made from pure silver. His monetary reform organized the currency around the silver penny.

more-religion-public.rationale: Charlemagne made tithes, baptism and observance of the Christian calendar legal duties and directed monasteries and episcopal churches to provide instruction.

national-self-determination.rationale: He conquered the Lombard kingdom and subjected the Saxons to Frankish rule. His succession ordinance assigns both territories to his sons as parts of his own realm.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Charlemagne used his royal authority to prescribe church instruction and regulate staple prices during famine.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: He required benefice holders to feed their serfs before selling surplus grain.

one-spouse-at-a-time.rationale: Chapter 42 of the Admonitio generalis bars a dismissed wife from marrying while her husband lives and bars a man from marrying another woman while his first wife lives.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: The 802 edict required laymen and clergy throughout his realm to swear personal fidelity to him as emperor and spelled out the service and obedience that the oath required.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Einhard records that Charlemagne had old vernacular songs about earlier kings committed to writing and began work on a grammar of his native language.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: He directly decreed maximum grain and bread prices in 794.

religion-from-peoples-character.rationale: Charlemagne imposed Christianity on the Saxons through his baptism decree and prohibited some of their ancestral religious rites.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: The Frankfurt capitulary rejects the Adoptionist teaching associated with Elipandus and Felix, and the Admonitio orders bishops and priests to teach the Catholic faith to the people.

religious-exemptions.rationale: The Saxon capitulary applies Christian fast observance and tithes in Saxony and penalizes refusal of baptism. The exception to the fasting rule rests on necessity as assessed by a priest.

religious-nation.rationale: Einhard records that accepting Christianity was a term of the Saxon settlement that joined Saxons and Franks as one people. The Saxon capitulary makes Christian baptism compulsory.

religious-offensive-war.rationale: The revised royal annals report that Charlemagne launched the 775 Saxon offensive with submission to Christianity as an explicit objective. His Saxon capitulary later enforced compulsory baptism.

remove-indigenous-peoples.rationale: The royal annals report that in 804 he took Saxon inhabitants from beyond the Elbe and from Wihmodi to Francia, including their families, and gave the trans-Elbe districts to the Obodrites.

return-to-pre-conversion-religion.rationale: The Saxon capitulary requires baptism and penalizes ancestral pagan practices, including cremation conducted as a pagan rite.

right-to-secede.rationale: The 806 succession plan disposes of Saxony as part of the realm to be handed down to his sons. Charlemagne repeatedly used force against Saxon attempts to break free after submission.

separate-church-state.rationale: Charlemagne used royal law to impose compulsory baptism and tithes, protect church sanctuary and penalize deliberate violation of the Lenten fast.

separated-powers.rationale: The 802 capitulary makes imperial envoys enforce royal law and requires them to refer cases they and the counts cannot resolve to the emperor for final judgment.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Charlemagne used his public authority to mandate Catholic preaching and to require the oath of loyalty to include service to God.

state-harmful.rationale: Charlemagne maintained royal courts and officials and sent his envoys throughout the kingdom to investigate injustice and enforce royal law.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The royal education order directed episcopal and monastic schools to teach psalms, chant and the calculation of the liturgical calendar.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: Charlemagne used law to support Christian worship, schooling and conduct. The Admonitio generalis commands Catholic preaching and Sunday observance.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Charlemagne used chapter 16 of the 802 capitulary to supervise the selection of candidates for ordination. At Frankfurt he and the synod also required unresolved ecclesiastical cases to be referred to him with the metropolitan’s report.

taxation-theft.rationale: The 802 capitulary makes payment of public dues part of the obligations owed under his imperial oath. Nijmegen confirms established tolls while suppressing newly invented exactions.

territorial-expansion.rationale: He took the Lombard kingship after defeating Desiderius and incorporated Saxony into the realm apportioned in his 806 succession plan.

work-for-welfare.rationale: The 806 Nijmegen capitulary directs lords to maintain their own poor dependents and forbids others from giving to itinerant beggars unless they work with their hands.

notes: The November 18 pass completed the current statement bank from the committed audit and checked earlier answers against the wording in force. It reviewed Einhard’s Life, the Royal Frankish Annals, the 789 Admonitio generalis, both Saxon capitularies, the 794 Frankfurt capitulary, the 802 general capitulary, the 806 Nijmegen and succession ordinances, the royal estate instructions, the 812 order concerning Hispani immigrants and letters to Baugulf and Michael I. The searches for the thinner themes covered famine and climate, livestock and forest rules, coinage, schooling, court procedure, marriage rules, military obligations, the Saxon campaigns and the peace negotiations with Byzantium. The 797 Saxon capitulary uses fines and local adjudication for some matters addressed under the earlier regime, with provisions for the king to demand higher fines in specified circumstances. Evidence was checked across economy, government, society, world affairs, liberty, culture, ecology, technology, means and globalism. The record is strongest on royal government, religious conformity, military expansion and relief during scarcity. Modern institutional questions and general policy claims beyond the scope of individual measures remain unknown.
